Reading notes

Books I have read:

Harbour Manners - by Ada Rivers

how strongly I recommend it: 7/10

ISBN: 0000000000

date read: 2024-03-01

A made-up summary in a highlighted box above the notes. Some book-notes sites print one like this. It should open the imported article.

The harbour town keeps its manners the way it keeps its boats. Everything is scraped and painted and tied up long before anyone thinks to ask about it. The work is done early so that nobody ever has to watch it being done.

Nobody talks about the tide directly because the tide is a shared worry. Shared worries are spoken of sideways and in a low voice. A direct question about the tide is treated as a small rudeness that people forgive but do not forget.

A neighbour who waves twice is being friendly and a neighbour who waves once is being polite. A neighbour who does not wave at all is simply mending a net and will wave twice tomorrow to make up for it.

The bakery queue is a parliament with no speaker. Everyone knows whose turn it is and nobody is ever wrong about it. Anyone who tries to skip ahead is not told off but is served last with great and terrible politeness.

Visitors are welcomed warmly and watched carefully and forgiven slowly. The whole process takes roughly ten years. After that a visitor becomes a newcomer and newcomers are allowed to complain about visitors.

Weather opens every conversation because it lets two people agree on something at once. The weather itself does not matter very much. What matters is the small moment of agreement that lets the real conversation begin.

To complain properly you must first apologise and then complain and then apologise again. Then you thank the person you complained to. Done well the whole thing takes a minute and leaves both people feeling slightly better.

The harbour master owns no boat. That is exactly why everyone trusts the harbour master with theirs. A harbour master with a boat would have opinions about moorings and nobody wants opinions about moorings.

Gossip travels along the sea wall faster than the wind. It always arrives a little kinder than it left because each person who passes it on smooths one rough edge. By the far end of the wall it is nearly a compliment.

Every house has a kettle by the window. Whoever is making tea can then keep an eye on the water. A boat coming in late is noticed by a dozen kettles before it reaches the harbour mouth.

When a storm comes the town gets quieter and not louder. The quiet is a kind of help that everyone offers and nobody names. People check on each other by leaving lights on in windows that face the street.

Children learn knots before they learn their times tables. They remember the knots longer too. A child who can tie a bowline in the dark is thought to be well brought up whatever their spelling is like.

The pub has one rule that was never written down. You buy a round for the table you joined and not for the table you left. Breaking the rule is not punished but it is remembered for a very long time.

A good fisherman never says the catch was good. The most he will say is that it could have been worse. Everyone understands the code and adjusts their prices at the market by morning.

Old sweaters are passed down like heirlooms and darned at the elbows. They are worn with a pride that nobody admits to. A sweater with three generations of darning is worth more than a new coat.

The ferry is always late and the timetable is always hopeful. Both are treated as old friends who cannot be expected to change. Complaining about the ferry is allowed but only to people who also take the ferry.

Lending a boat is easy and borrowing one is hard. Returning one cleaner than you found it is the whole of good manners. A borrowed boat returned dirty ends a friendship more surely than any argument.

The lighthouse keeper writes a letter to the town every winter. The town answers it every spring in the same newspaper column. Nobody remembers when the letters began and nobody would dream of letting them stop.
